author: Tampa Bay Times
title: Pinellas judge rules in favor of SPCA in Waddles case - NewsBreak
text:
3 hours ago Jeane Newton of Tampa shows off her support for Waddles before the start of proceedings at the Pinellas County Criminal Justice Center. [ DOUGLAS R. CLIFFORD | Times ] You can lead a pig to shelter, but you can’t make him go into the shade.
That’s basically what Pinellas County Court Judge Kathleen Hessinger said Wednesday when she ruled that the SPCA of Tampa Bay did not neglect a 350-pound pig named Waddles.
“This pig got sunburned,” the judge said. “Somebody has to be taken down. So the county decides the SPCA did. But sometimes bad things happen in life. No one here has done anything wrong.”
Judge Kathleen Hessinger was surprised by the crowd size and said she wished people showed the same passion over abused women and children. [ DOUGLAS R. CLIFFORD | Times ] People who packed the courtroom demanding “Justice for Waddles” disagreed. More than 80 filled the wooden pews. Another 20 watched from a separate courtroom.
The judge said that was the largest crowd she had ever seen.
In the last year, Waddles’ story has gone viral on social media. Millions of supporters from as far away as Australia have sent messages to the pig. He’s inspired T-shirts and TV appearances, petitions and protests , a cryptocurrency coin and a video game .
Animal advocates pack a courtroom to hear evidence in a case that might have had serious consequences for the SPCA shelter. [ DOUGLAS R. CLIFFORD | Times ] Alec Waid, attorney for the SPCA, discusses the details of a citation issued by Stephanie Nikodem, a former investigator with Pinellas County Animal Services. [ DOUGLAS R. CLIFFORD | Times ] Waddles, his supporters said, had been left in the summer sun at the SPCA for two weeks. There was a barn in his pasture, but he couldn’t get inside. By the time a rescuer came to get him, his body was covered in oozing blisters.
Someone saw the pig inside that barn, said Alec Waid, the SPCA’s lawyer. Outside, Waddles had shade from the building and mud pits to cool off in. “The SPCA did what it could,” Waid said. “We’re left with some sort of skin condition. But there’s zero evidence that it was caused by inadequate shelter.”
Last summer, the county charged the SPCA with animal cruelty, a civil citation. If the judge had ruled against the nonprofit, the shelter might have had to shut down.
After nine witnesses and four hours of testimony, Hessinger took another hour to come back with her ruling.
“An animal is, by definition, a dumb creature,” the judge said. “But they get out of the sun when they’re hot. It doesn’t take a vet tech to tell him that he’s getting sunburned.”
Waddles was 6 months old when a Seminole family adopted him and brought him into their home. He was pink, with white tufts of hair and a long, curly tail. So small his human mom could cradle him in her arms.
They thought he’d grow to the size of a big dog. But in two years, he weighed 200 pounds.
Waddles the pig, shown in April, got a new covered area able to protect his sensitive skin after new owner Connie Pavelich helped nurse him back to health at her home in Lithia. [ LUIS SANTANA | Times ] After losing their cleaning business and getting flooded by two hurricanes, the family had to move in with relatives in Branson, Missouri. And find a new home for Waddles.
They couldn’t find anyplace that would take the pig. Not even Pinellas Animal Services.
“No one wanted him,” the judge said. “Maybe he was too fat. Maybe he had too many issues.”
She read text messages from Waddles’ original owner, begging the shelter to take the pig, agonizing over how to transport him, saying his hoofs were overgrown and his skin was itchy. The SPCA did what it’s supposed to, the judge said. It took in this animal no one else would. “No good deed goes unpunished.”
Once the SPCA agreed to accept Waddles, its owner had no way of getting him there. On the day her house was supposed to be sold, the real estate agent testified, he rented a U-Haul and got a friend to help him move the pig.
What did the pig look like? asked county attorney David Barrera.
“Like a regular pig,” said Michael Coup. “Just a pig. A really big pig.”
His back wasn’t red or blistered, Coup said. He didn’t appear sunburned. Just a little muddy.
“You don’t really know anything about pigs, do you?” the SPCA’s lawyer countered.
The real estate agent looked confused, then laughed. “Well, not in a professional farmer-type way, no.”
An animal abuse investigator from Indiana testified via Zoom that the SPCA wasn’t negligent. “Peeling skin could be from stress, from hay, allergies,” Kim Wolsiffer said. “The transport itself contributed to the stress.”
An animal abuse investigator from Pinellas County said the pig couldn’t move out of the sun or roll over in the mud to keep the top of his body cool. “This pig was quite obese,” Joseph Birch said. “If the pig isn’t going into that shelter, a person needs to intervene. Instead, he continued to suffer.”
Saying that Waddles should have known to get himself into the barn, Birch said, “would be like if my dog had an infection and I just left the medicine out for him, but he never ate it. That isn’t solving the situation.”
Kelly Dill, who rescued Waddles through her Pork Butt Pastures, testified that the pig’s condition was “awful. Horrific. All his skin had peeled off, and it was just raw skin.” The worst shape she’d ever seen a pig in. “I absolutely was not comfortable leaving him at the SPCA,” she said.
The SPCA’s lawyer argued that there was no proof the photos she had sent to animal control or the veterinarian hadn’t been doctored, and criticized her for putting the pig in a cage to load into her van.
Dill’s eyes widened. “How do you think pigs get transported?”
The judge’s favorite witness, she said, was the “country veterinarian” who saw Waddles weeks after he’d been taken from the SPCA, when he was doing much better. Pigs, Larry Bailey testified, “can make some decisions for themselves, but not preventative ones. He might not know to come out of the sun to prevent sunburn. Even people can’t do that.”
The audience laughed, because Bailey himself looked sunburned.
Veterinarian Larry Bailey testifies about examining Waddles after the pig's sun exposure. [ DOUGLAS R. CLIFFORD | Times ] Later, when she read her ruling, the judge said of the vet: “He was sunburned from top to bottom. I guess no one pushed him into the barn to get shade.”
That’s when Waddles’ new owner, Connie Pavelich, walked out of the courtroom, wiping her eyes. She had spent the last year trying to help the pig heal, sharing his story, feeding him zucchini and watermelon.
Afterward, outside the courthouse, she looked shaken. “Guess we lost because the vet was sunburned,” she said.
Martha Boden, the SPCA’s CEO, hugged her lawyers after the verdict. “We’re very pleased,” she said. “We’ve maintained for a year that we did great work for this pig.”
The shelter, she said, stopped taking farm animals after Waddles left and hasn’t decided if they will accept them in the future.
